\chapter{Where You Came From}
\label{ch:ml-ablative}
\hlchaptermodality{83}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask where somebody is from and answer with any place I know.}

From cold: the from-word and what must precede it, the question it builds at no cost, and what a noun ending in -am does before any ending.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ninnŭ]{\ml{നിന്ന്} (ninnŭ) — from}

\label{lesson:ML-C83-ninnu}



\begin{quote}
Say the ending that means \textbf{in} or \textbf{at}. Then say the word for a town, and put that ending on it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: from is built on in}]
You can already say that something is \textbf{in} a place. This is how you say it comes \textbf{out of} one, and the useful part is that \textbf{you do not throw the old ending away.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഊരിൽ}} \emph{ūril} & in the town \\
\textbf{\ml{ഊരിൽ} \ml{നിന്ന്}} \emph{ūril ninnŭ} & \textbf{from} the town \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ml{നിന്ന്} goes after the word that already carries the in-ending.} So \emph{from} is not a new ending competing with the old one — it is a second step \textbf{on top of} it, and the sense follows the shape: \emph{in the town} first, then \emph{out of that}.

One thing is different from every ending you have met. The endings glue on: \emph{ūr} plus \emph{-il} is one written word. \textbf{\ml{നിന്ന്} is a word of its own}, standing after it. It began life as a form of a verb meaning \emph{to stand} — \emph{having stood in the town} — and hardened into the ordinary way to say \emph{from}. That history is why it behaves like a word and not like a suffix.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A direction, on top of a position.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ūril}
  \item \emph{ūril ninnŭ}
  \item which of the two is a position and which is a direction
  \item what has to already be on the word before \emph{ninnŭ} can follow it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ninnŭ} mean? (\textbf{From}.) What must come before it? (\textbf{The in-ending}.) And is it glued on or standing apart? (\textbf{Standing apart}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eviṭe ninnŭ]{\ml{എവിടെ} \ml{നിന്ന്} (eviṭe ninnŭ) — where from?}

\label{lesson:ML-C83-evide-ninnu}



\begin{quote}
Say the word that asks \textbf{where}. Then say the word that means \textbf{from}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{എവിടെ} \ml{നിന്ന്}}
\textbf{\ml{എവിടെ} \ml{നിന്ന്}?} — \emph{eviṭe ninnŭ?} — where from?

Put the two together in the order the last lesson gave you and the question builds itself. \textbf{\ml{എവിടെ}} already asks about a place you are \textbf{at}; \textbf{\ml{നിന്ന്}} turns that into a place you came \textbf{out of}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എവിടെ}?} & where? \\
\textbf{\ml{എവിടെ} \ml{നിന്ന്}?} & where \textbf{from}? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Nothing new is memorised here. \textbf{The question is two words you own, in the order the last lesson gave you}, and that is worth noticing in its own right: a well-built system spends its second question for free.

Answer it with any place you have:

\textbf{\ml{ഊരിൽ} \ml{നിന്ന്}} — \emph{ūril ninnŭ} — from the town.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both sides of an exchange, from one rule.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{eviṭe}, then \emph{eviṭe ninnŭ}
  \item what the second word did to the first
  \item \emph{ūril ninnŭ}
  \item the question, then your own answer to it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask \emph{where from}? (\emph{\textbf{eviṭe ninnŭ}}.) How many new words did that cost you? (\textbf{None} — both were already yours.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kēraḷattil]{\ml{കേരളത്തിൽ} (kēraḷattil) — what -\ml{ം} does before an ending}

\label{lesson:ML-C83-keralathil}



\begin{quote}
Say the name of the state and the name of the country. Then say the ending that means \textbf{in}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two of your place names behave differently}]
Put the in-ending on both names you learned and only one of them goes quietly.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{in it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}} & \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യയിൽ}} \emph{indyayil} \\
\textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} & \textbf{\ml{കേരളത്തിൽ}} \emph{kēraḷattil} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}} ends in \textbf{\ml{അ}} and takes a \textbf{-\ml{യ}-} to join, the same join \emph{kocciyil} uses. Nothing surprising. Which letter joins depends on which vowel the word ends in; \textbf{\ml{അ}} takes this one.

\textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} does something else. \textbf{The -\ml{ം} is gone and -\ml{ത്ത}- has arrived in its place}, and only then does the ending follow.

That is not this word being difficult. \textbf{Every noun ending in -\ml{ം} does it}, and this book has taught you a pile of them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{in it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{പുസ്തകം}} \emph{pustakaṁ} & \textbf{\ml{പുസ്തകത്തിൽ}} \emph{pustakattil} \\
\textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} \emph{kēraḷaṁ} & \textbf{\ml{കേരളത്തിൽ}} \emph{kēraḷattil} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So this is \textbf{a class, not an exception}, and it is a large one. Learning it once puts every \textbf{-\ml{ം}} word you own into the in-form, which is a much better return than memorising two place names.

\textbf{The -\ml{ം} is a citation dress.} It is what the word wears when it stands alone and is named; the moment \textbf{a case ending} is added, the word changes into its working shape first. Look for that habit rather than for a list.

\textbf{Other kinds of ending do other things to it.} You have met one already: the \emph{and} ending puts \textbf{\ml{വും}} there instead — \textbf{\ml{വെള്ളം}}, \textbf{\ml{വെള്ളവും}} — which is not this at all. What this chapter shows you is the case ending.

Now the whole chapter arrives at once:

\textbf{\ml{കേരളത്തിൽ} \ml{നിന്ന്}} — \emph{kēraḷattil ninnŭ} — \textbf{from Kerala.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{indyayil}, then \emph{kēraḷattil}
  \item which of the two changed more, and what happened to its ending
  \item \emph{pustakattil}
  \item \emph{kēraḷattil ninnŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to \textbf{-\ml{ം}} when a case ending is added? (\textbf{It is replaced by -\ml{ത്ത}-}.) Is that one word's quirk or a whole class? (\textbf{A whole class}.) And how do you say \emph{from Kerala}? (\emph{\textbf{kēraḷattil ninnŭ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[evide ninnŭ enna ōrmma]{(where you came from) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R83-from-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Ask \emph{where from}, then say what each of its two words was doing.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one position, one direction, one change of shape}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{in it} & \textbf{\textbf{from} it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഊര്}} & \textbf{\ml{ഊരിൽ}} & \textbf{\ml{ഊരിൽ} \ml{നിന്ന്}} \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യ}} & \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യയിൽ}} & \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ത്യയിൽ} \ml{നിന്ന്}} \\
\textbf{\ml{കേരളം}} & \textbf{\ml{കേരളത്തിൽ}} & \textbf{\ml{കേരളത്തിൽ} \ml{നിന്ന്}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the middle column and then the last. \textbf{\ml{നിന്ന്} never changes and never glues on} — it follows a word that already carries the in-ending, and it does the same thing to all three.

Read the first column against the middle and the third row is the odd one. \textbf{\ml{കേരളം} loses its -\ml{ം} and puts -\ml{ത്ത}- there instead}, and so does every other \textbf{-\ml{ം}} word this book has given you. \textbf{The -\ml{ം} is a citation dress}: what the word wears standing alone, dropped the moment \textbf{a case ending} is added.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
An answer to the first question anybody asks you.

Two chapters ago the place words arrived and the question was still unaskable. Now both halves exist, and \textbf{neither the question nor most of the answer cost a new word}: \emph{eviṭe ninnŭ} is two words you owned, and the in-form of every -\ml{ം} noun came out of a single rule rather than a list.

That is the shape worth carrying: \textbf{when the endings are regular, the work is in knowing which shape a word takes before an ending, not in learning more endings.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{eviṭe ninnŭ?}
  \item \emph{ūril ninnŭ}
  \item \emph{indyayil ninnŭ}
  \item \emph{kēraḷattil ninnŭ}
  \item which of those three changed its shape before the ending, and what it changed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What must a word carry before \emph{ninnŭ}? (\textbf{The in-ending}.) What replaces \textbf{-\ml{ം}} before an ending? (\textbf{-\ml{ത്ത}-}.) And how do you say \emph{from Kerala}? (\emph{\textbf{kēraḷattil ninnŭ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
